habitat: On soil under oak, beech, birch and conifers, often after summer rain.
lookalikes: Jack-o’-lantern / tsukiyotake (Omphalotus) grows in clusters on wood with true gills; false chanterelle has thin, orange, forked gills.

habitat: Under spruce, pine, birch and oak; sponge pores instead of gills.
lookalikes: Bitter bolete (pinkish pores, dark net on stem) ruins a dish; red-pored boletes that bruise blue can be toxic.

habitat: Spring, around dying elms, old orchards, burn sites and river woods. Himalayan morels in Nepal, India and Pakistan.
lookalikes: False morel (Gyromitra) is deadly: brain-like, wrinkled cap and not hollow inside. Always slice true morels in half: they are fully hollow. Never eat raw.

habitat: Large rosettes at the base of old oaks.
lookalikes: Black-staining polypore is similar but harmless; low-risk if it grows from oak and is fresh.

habitat: Bright orange-yellow shelves on oak, cherry and willow.
lookalikes: Specimens on yew, eucalyptus or conifers have caused illness. Cook well and try a small amount first.

habitat: Shelving clusters on dead hardwood; the winter oyster likes cold snaps.
lookalikes: Tsukiyotake (Omphalotus japonicus) in Japan glows and has a dark stain at the stem base, and is Japan’s most common poisoning. Angel wings (sugihiratake) on conifer stumps has killed people. In Australia, ghost fungus is toxic.

habitat: White icicle-like clumps on wounded hardwood trees.
lookalikes: Few dangerous lookalikes. Related Hericium species are also edible.

habitat: Lawns, roadsides and disturbed ground. Eat within hours because it dissolves into ink.
lookalikes: Common ink cap (Coprinopsis atramentaria) causes a severe reaction with alcohol taken within days of eating it.

habitat: Pastures and field edges; white ball the size of a melon.
lookalikes: Slice every puffball top to bottom. Any outline of a cap and gills inside means a deadly Amanita button. Earthballs are firm and purple-black inside.

habitat: Under red pine in Japan and Korea, and in Scandinavian pine forest and the Pacific Northwest. Spicy-cinnamon smell. Japanese matsutake hills are usually leased, so picking there without permission is theft.
lookalikes: Amanita smithiana (Pacific Northwest) causes kidney failure. Check for a bulb, a sac at the stem base and the absence of the matsutake smell.

habitat: On fallen konara oak and chinquapin logs in spring and autumn.
lookalikes: Tsukiyotake grows on similar wood: dark stain inside the stem base and glowing gills.

habitat: Winter clusters of orange caps with velvety dark stems on hardwood stumps.
lookalikes: Funeral bell (Galerina marginata) is deadly and grows on the same stumps. Take a spore print every time: rusty brown means Galerina, white means enoki.

habitat: Slimy orange caps on beech and oak stumps in Japanese mountains.
lookalikes: Funeral bell (Galerina) on the same wood is deadly. Beginners should not pick small brown mushrooms on wood.

habitat: Big clusters at tree bases. Must be cooked thoroughly, and some people react even then.
lookalikes: Funeral bell (Galerina) and sulphur tuft (Hypholoma) form similar clusters. Honey fungus has a white spore print and a ring.

habitat: Lilac mushrooms in leaf litter and compost, late in the season.
lookalikes: Violet webcaps (Cortinarius) have rusty-brown spores and a cobweb veil, and some kill. Blewit spores are pale pink.

habitat: Grazed meadows after warm rain; pink gills turning chocolate brown.
lookalikes: Destroying angel (white gills, sac at the base) is deadly. Yellow stainer turns chrome yellow at the stem base and smells of ink.

habitat: Tall, snakeskin-patterned stem with a movable ring; grassland and woodland edges.
lookalikes: Green-spored parasol (Chlorophyllum molybdites) is the most common cause of mushroom poisoning in North America and is spreading in Japan. Small Lepiota species are deadly. Take a spore print: green means don’t eat.

habitat: Under pine, including introduced pine plantations in Australia, NZ, Chile and South Africa. Bleeds carrot-orange milk.
lookalikes: Woolly milk cap and other milk caps with white milk are toxic. Edible ones bleed orange and slowly turn green.

habitat: Slimy brown cap under pine; common in southern-hemisphere pine plantations. Peel the cap.
lookalikes: Few dangerous lookalikes, but it upsets some stomachs. Discard soggy or old specimens.

habitat: Teeth instead of gills under the cap; mixed woods.
lookalikes: One of the safest beginner species: few lookalikes have spines.

habitat: Hollow dark funnels in moss under beech and oak; hard to spot.
lookalikes: Low risk. Make sure it is hollow and has no gills.

habitat: Mossy conifer forests late in the season, in large troops.
lookalikes: Small brown gilled mushrooms nearby can be deadly. Check the hollow yellow stem and blunt false gills.

habitat: Rubbery brown ears on dead elder and hardwood; fruits almost year-round in wet climates.
lookalikes: Few dangerous lookalikes. Avoid specimens that are hard or brittle when wet.

habitat: Rises from termite mounds after the first heavy rains; prized across Africa and South/Southeast Asia.
lookalikes: Deadly Amanitas and green-spored parasol fruit in the same season. Check the long rooting stem connected to the mound.

habitat: Ruffled cream mass at the base of pines.
lookalikes: Few lookalikes. Clean it well because it traps grit.

habitat: Orange cap rising out of a white egg-like sac; warm oak and pine woods.
lookalikes: Experts only. It is an Amanita, and deadly relatives look like it at the egg stage. Never eat one picked as an unopened egg.

habitat: Underground with oak and hazel in southern Europe; found with dogs. Usually on private or licensed land.
lookalikes: Low risk. Chinese truffles are sometimes sold as fakes.

habitat: Rings in spring grassland and hedgerows; mealy smell.
lookalikes: Deadly fibrecap (Inocybe erubescens) and the livid pinkgill fruit at the same time and place.

habitat: Bright orange crust parasitising milk caps in North American forests.
lookalikes: Discard soft or decaying specimens. The host underneath can’t be identified.

habitat: With oak and other hardwoods; introduced to California, Canberra and Melbourne, Chile and South Africa.
lookalikes: Causes most mushroom deaths worldwide. Greenish cap, white gills, a ring and a cup-shaped sac at the base. Symptoms appear 6–24 hours later, after the liver damage has begun.

habitat: Pure white Amanita in woodland.
lookalikes: Mistaken for field mushrooms, puffball buttons and white edibles. One cap can kill.

habitat: Small brown caps on rotting wood.
lookalikes: Contains the same toxins as the death cap. Confused with enoki, honey fungus and nameko.

habitat: Orange-brown caps in conifer and mixed woods.
lookalikes: Destroys the kidneys. Symptoms can take 2–20 days, so the link is often missed.

habitat: Spring conifer woods, at the same time as morels.
lookalikes: Brain-like cap, chambered (not hollow) inside. Toxic even after cooking, and the fumes are dangerous.

habitat: Clusters on wood or buried roots; gills may glow in the dark.
lookalikes: Severe vomiting. Mistaken for chanterelles, oysters and shiitake.

habitat: Lawns and parks in warm climates; forms large rings.
lookalikes: Looks like an edible parasol. Spore print is green. Causes violent illness.

habitat: Red finger-like growths at the base of oak stumps in Japan and Korea.
lookalikes: Deadly if eaten and irritates the skin, so do not touch it.

habitat: Red cap with white warts under birch and pine, including southern-hemisphere pine plantations.
lookalikes: Toxic. White warts can wash off in rain, which makes it look like other red-capped species.

habitat: Grey-cream caps in broadleaf woods.
lookalikes: One of Japan’s most common poisonings. Mistaken for edible shimeji and St George’s mushroom; the spores are pink.

habitat: Dense sulphur-yellow clusters on stumps almost all year.
lookalikes: Mistaken for honey fungus. Very bitter, with greenish gills.
